paper_title: Loupe: Reinforcing Knowledge-Intensive Video Generation Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video generation models [4, 23, 25] have advanced rapidly in visual fidelity and motion quality. However, knowledge-intensive video generation [33, 44] remains challenging because requests often omit the factual details, distinctive appearances, and temporal relationships needed to depict named entity, event, or process. Consequently, generators may produce visually compelling videos while hallucinating entities, misrepresenting appearances, or depicting incorrect event sequences  (Fig.1)  . Improving rendering capabilities alone cannot address these knowledge gaps. Equipping video generation agents [10, 16, 18] with search tools offers promising solution. However, effective evidence acquisition requires agents to identify knowledge gaps, formulate queries, verify information, select visual references, and integrate evidence into coherent generation plans. Existing prompt-based workflows rely largely on manually designed strategies, limiting adaptive search and evidence reasoning. This motivates learning agents that can make effective search and planning decisions. However, training such agents introduces credit assignment challenge. Conventional supervised finetuning (SFT) treats assistant tokens uniformly despite varying decision quality, while reinforcement learning (RL) based on final-video feedback is costly and entangles agent decisions with the generators rendering ability. Moreover, trajectory-level rewards obscure individual step contributions. Recent methods [22, 38] explore process supervision through answer-backtracked clues or rubrics derived from correctness-contrasted reasoning trajectories. However, knowledge-intensive video requests typically lack annotated factual answers or target videos, making such supervision particularly difficult to obtain directly in practice. Our key insight is that request specifies what must be verified, even when the corresponding answers are unknown. It may require identifying an entity, establishing factual details, grounding its appearance, and preserving event order without providing the answers. These requirements define evaluation criteria rather than factual answers, which must be acquired through external evidence. Combining request-derived criteria with interaction history enables us to evaluate intermediate decisions without requiring annotated factual answers or target videos. Based on this insight, we present Loupe, video generation agent that retrieves and integrates external evidence into grounded generation inputs  (Fig.2)  . Loupe identifies knowledge gaps and iteratively uses text search, image search, and web browsing to acquire and verify evidence, producing temporally coherent video prompts and supporting reference images for downstream generators. To train Loupe, we introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which evaluates intermediate decisions against request-derived requirements and retrieved evidence. For each prompt, RBC constructs rubric comprising reference requirements, specifying the entities, facts, visual attributes, and temporal relations to establish, and grounding types, characterizing associated knowledge needs. process judge evaluates each assistant step using the rubric and interaction history, assigning credit according to its contribution to evidence acquisition and utilization. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistanttoken loss according to normalized step credits, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-specific credits into relative advantage estimation across corresponding turn positions, alongside final reward for the completed video plan and reference images. Both rewards are evaluated without video rendering. To evaluate knowledge-intensive video generation, we construct Search-VBench, dedicated benchmark comprising 150 held-out prompts across seven categories, 339 reference images, and 566 evaluation rubric items. It measures faithfulness, visual correctness, temporal dynamics, and aesthetics. Experiments demonstrate that Loupe improves all four dimensions across three video generators, raising MiniMax-H3s [23] overall score from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Human evaluations yield an overall preference rate of 82.33, while evaluations on SciVBench [44] and KIVI-Bench [33] demonstrate gains in scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Moreover, ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT 2 followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce Loupe, an evidence-driven video generation agent that retrieves and verifies external textual and visual evidence to produce grounded temporal prompts and reference images across multiple generators. We propose Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), request-conditioned process supervision framework that derives evaluation criteria without annotated factual answers. Together with RBC-SFT and RBC-GRPO, it enables step-level supervision in supervised and reinforcement learning without video rendering during training. We construct Search-VBench, dedicated benchmark for knowledge-intensive video generation, and demonstrate Loupes effectiveness across multiple video generators, benchmarks, and human evaluations.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agentic image generation. Early systems such as GenArtist [35] and GEMS [15] rely on prompt-based workflows. Gen-Searcher [9] learns search-augmented generation with textual and image feedback. Loupe extends evidence acquisition to video, where retrieved knowledge must support actions, state changes, and temporal relationships, and supervises search and planning before rendering. Agentic video generation. Existing systems explore task decomposition, staged planning, and external tools [10, 16, 19, 36]. AgenticGen [6] optimizes advertising strategy selection and draft generation using business performance. VideoGen-Agent [18] learns tool coordination through SFT and RL, with rewards incorporating generated-video quality. In contrast, Loupe focuses on external evidence acquisition and temporal planning, using step-level credits and final planning reward without rendering videos during RL. Process supervision and credit assignment. Prior work explores information gain, critical-step verification, and intermediate evidence structures for search agents [20, 21, 27, 34]. ABSeeker [22] backtracks from known correct answers to construct supervision clues for search steps, while SRaR [38] derives rubrics from answer-verified correct and incorrect reasoning trajectories and combines process feedback with answer-based rewards. Unlike ABSeeker and SRaR, whose original supervision construction relies on known answers or answer-verified trajectories, Loupe derives verification requirements directly from user requests and evaluates individual agent decisions against these requirements and retrieved evidence, enabling process supervision without annotated factual answers or target videos.

sections.title: 3.2 Rubric-Based Credit
sections.content: Evaluating only the final plan or the video leaves the contribution of earlier search steps unresolved. We observe that video can be realized in multiple correct ways, yet it must satisfy set of verifiable factual, appearance, and temporal requirements. sections.content: Training Details. We use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [5] as the agent backbone. RBC-SFT is trained on approximately 16K filtered teacher trajectories, and RBC-GRPO is initialized from this checkpoint using separate pool of 2K prompts. GLM-5.3-Flash [43] serves as the process judge. We use AdamW with learning rates of 105 (SFT) and 106 (RL), and batch size 16. Each RL prompt has six rollouts, up to ten interaction turns, five returned images per turn, 36K context length, and 4K response limit per turn. Overlong and repetitive rollouts are masked. Sci-VBench [44] evaluates Visual Quality (VT), Spatiotemporal Consistency (SC), Prompt Grounding (PG), and Scientific and Causal Correctness (SCC); we report its native average score. KIVI-Bench [33] evaluates 60-second videos in terms of Factual Precision (FactP), Relevance (Rel), Completeness (Cmp), Clarity (Clr), and Helpfulness (HelpS). Some results are re-evaluated using the official repository. We compare direct generation and Loupe under identical generator and inference settings. MiniMax-H3, Wan 3.0, and Seedance 2.0 are evaluated on SearchVBench and Sci-VBench, while KIVI-Bench uses MiniMax-H3 due to generation costs. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Loupe, an evidence-driven video generation agent that retrieves and integrates external textual and visual evidence to address knowledge gaps in video generation. To enable effective agent learning, we introduced Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which evaluates intermediate search and planning decisions against prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements. Building on RBC, we developed RBC-SFT and RBC-GRPO to incorporate fine-grained process supervision into supervised and reinforcement learning without video rendering during RL. We also constructed SearchVBench and demonstrated consistent improvements across multiple video generators and external benchmarks, with ablations validating the effectiveness of RBC training. Overall, our work highlights the importance of external evidence acquisition, grounded temporal planning, and request-conditioned process supervision for advancing knowledge-intensive video generation.

D.2 Quantifying RBC Judge Noise As RBC relies on an LLM-based process reward model, its scoring reliability may be affected by inherent judgment variability. Moreover, the adjustment ranges in Tab.1 are manually specified, making it important to assess the stability and accuracy of the resulting credits. We conduct two complementary evaluations. First, we randomly sample 1K trajectories and ask the RBC Judge to independently score each step three times. We define self-consistency as the proportion of steps whose maximum and minimum assigned credits differ by at most 0.1. Under this criterion, the judge achieves 93.6% self-consistency, indicating stable scoring across repeated evaluations. Second, we randomly sample 100 steps for manual evaluation by five independent annotators. We measure Judge-human agreement as the proportion of comparisons in which the judge-assigned and humanassigned credits differ by at most 0.1. The resulting agreement reaches 91.8% across 500 comparisons, further supporting the reliability of our rubric-based scoring scheme. Overall, these results suggest that the RBC Judge provides stable and reasonably accurate step-level supervision, with limited sensitivity to repeated judgments. D.3 Training Overhead of RBC Scoring Time Analysis. The complete training pipeline consists of four stages: video prompt and rubric generation, teacher trajectory collection, RBC-SFT, and RBC-GRPO. Generating 25K video prompts and rubrics takes approximately 17 hours (20 per prompt, concurrency 8), while collecting teacher trajectories takes approximately 70 hours (160 per trajectory, concurrency 16). For RBC-SFT, scoring the collected trajectories requires approximately 13 hours (30 per trajectory, concurrency 16), followed by 10 hours of training for two epochs. Thus, RBC scoring introduces an additional 13 hours compared with standard SFT. For RBC-GRPO, we asynchronously overlap step-level judging with subsequent response generation, keeping the parameter update time nearly identical to standard GRPO (700 per update). Training for 125 steps takes approximately 25 hours. Overall, the complete pipeline takes approximately 135 hours (5.6 days), with the additional RBC scoring overhead accounting for only 13 hours (9.6%). Cost Analysis. We further analyze the computational cost of RBC-based supervision. The RBC judge uses GLM-5.3-Flash for step-level scoring, Gemini 3.1 Pro is mainly used for prompt construction and teacher trajectory collection, and training incurs additional GPU cost. The RBC judge accounts for less than 10% of the overall pipeline cost, demonstrating that fine-grained process supervision introduces limited overhead. For each backbone (MiniMax-H3, Wan 3.0, and Seedance 2.0), we evaluated 100 pairs comparing direct generation with Loupe-augmented generation. Five raters independently assessed each pair, with model identities hidden and the leftright order randomized. For each pair, raters selected their preferred video separately for Faithfulness, Visual Correctness, Temporal Dynamics, Aesthetics, and Overall quality, without tie option. This protocol yielded 500 rater-pair assessments per backbone and 1,500 assessments in total, each comprising five dimension-specific choices. 20 For each dimension, the Loupe preference rate was computed as the fraction of individual rater choices favoring Loupe (500 choices per backbone; 1,500 pooled). D.5 Additional Qualitative Comparisons Additional qualitative video comparisons are provided in Fig.S1Fig.S4, covering knowledge dynamic visualization, culture, ritual, and sport motion, long-tail entity motion, and procedural how-to generation. Each figure presents five sampled frames per video to illustrate both visual content and temporal progression. These examples examine complementary challenges: animating botanical illustrations 21 with taxonomic annotations, revealing specific textile patterns and handwritten information, coordinating interactions among named characters, and presenting an ordered reimbursement workflow with readable interface labels. Across these cases, baseline generators often reproduce the broad setting or action while missing finer requirements, such as distinctive character appearances, the requested number of participants, or legible task-specific text. Our results generally show clearer differentiation of the requested entities and closer correspondence between the evolving scene and the information specified in the prompt. The comparisons also reveal remaining limitations: fine-grained attributes can still deviate from the request, as illustrated by the hair-color mismatch in Fig.S4, and readable generated annotations alone do not establish factual correctness. Together, these examples illustrate both the improvements and the remaining challenges in maintaining entity-specific details and semantic constraints throughout video generation.

sections.title: F Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Loupe depends on the availability and reliability of retrieved evidence, and well-grounded plans do not guarantee faithful rendering by downstream video generators. RBC uses rubric-based model judgments to assess individual decisions; these judgments provide scalable supervision but may not capture every aspect of decision quality. Future work could improve evidence verification and investigate human-guided calibration of process feedback. 22 Figure S1. Qualitative comparison on Knowledge Dynamic Visualization. sections.title: G Prompts and Annotation Instructions
sections.content: This section collects the prompts used for seed prompt rewriting, Loupes search and video planning, RBC step scoring, final-plan outcome evaluation, and Search-VBench video evaluation. The blue boxes present the prompt text and, where applicable, input templates with placeholders for sample-specific metadata, model outputs, and media. RBC step scoring evaluates individual assistant actions, finalplan evaluation assesses the textual generation plan and reference-image choices, and Search-VBench evaluates generated videos for faithfulness, visual correctness, temporal dynamics, and aesthetics. G.1 Seed Prompt Rewriting

sections.title: Seed Prompt Rewriting

sections.title: Loupe System Prompt
sections.content: You transform user video intent into factually grounded, temporally coherent video-generation prompt. Follow this process: (1) analyze the intent using logic, common sense and visual reasoning; (2) identify the specific knowledge gaps that could change what appears or how the event unfolds; (3) search only for those gaps when external retrieval is useful; (4) check that the evidence resolves them; and (5) output detailed, staged video prompt covering the complete requested content and process. Search is optional: skip it for ordinary scenes and reliable common knowledge. However, for visually distinctive named entities, consider image_search even when their identity is already known, since video model may not reproduce their appearance reliably from the name alone. Core behavior Reason naturally about: * what information is required to generate the video correctly; * what can be handled reliably using general world knowledge; * what requires external grounding; * whether text search, image search, or browsing is useful; * what the retrieved evidence establishes; * how the knowledge should manifest as entities, actions, interactions, state changes, causal relations, and temporal progression in the video. Response protocol In every ordinary round output exactly one of these, with no surrounding text: <think>brief current knowledge state and next action</think><tool_call>...</tool_call> or <think>brief final planning decision</think><answer>...</answer>. Never emit more than one tool call or combine tool call with an answer. Use only as many tool calls as are genuinely necessary, never repeat query, and after each tool result reassess whether another call is genuinely useful. If no retrieval is needed, answer immediately in the first round. If tool fails, do not blindly repeat the same call; use another query/tool only if it can resolve necessary uncertainty, otherwise answer.
